html:
How an AI reading loop forced me to finally bring my house — my mind — in order

Act I — The Loop That Wouldn’t Stop

It started, like most dangerous things in my life, with a good idea.

I had built a reading loop — AI-assisted, naturally. Every morning I would feed articles into Claude, ask it to summarise, extract insights, and suggest what I should write next. Then I’d draft a piece. Claude would refine it. I’d publish. The loop was elegant. The loop was productive. The loop was, I told myself, the future of knowledge work.

What I didn’t notice — not for the first few weeks, anyway — was that the loop had a flaw baked into its very elegance.

I was reading more than ever. Writing more than ever. But I had quietly stopped finishing things. A Medium draft sat at 80% for eleven days. A GitHub repo that needed three more commits gathered dust. An email to my cross-geo team about the upcoming PI planning sat as a red unread reminder in my own inbox.

I had optimised the intake. I had forgotten to optimise the output.

That sentence — scribbled in the margin of a notebook while waiting for a CI pipeline to finish — became the pivot point of everything that followed.

Act II — The Cheatsheet on the Wall

A colleague shared Dr. Miro Bada’s infographic: How to Master Time Management — The Cheatsheet to Win Back Your Time. Fifteen frameworks on a single page. I had seen most of them before, scattered across blog posts and productivity books. But seeing them all together, in one visual, did something different to my brain.

It felt like walking into a cluttered room and suddenly having someone turn on all the lights at once.

I printed it. I stuck it on the wall beside my monitor. And for the first time in weeks, I stopped reading and started looking — really looking — at how I was spending my hours.

Here is what I found, and here is what I did about it.

Act III — Fifteen Mirrors, One Reflection

1. The Domino Effect — Stop Starting, Start Sequencing

My calendar was a museum of parallel beginnings. Three architectural documents in draft. Two LinkedIn posts half-written. One book chapter stalled at a metaphor I couldn’t crack.

The Domino Effect asks a simple question: which task, when completed, makes the next one easier? I restructured my week around this logic. The PI planning summary first — because it unblocked five team leads. The Medium article second — because finishing it cleared the mental noise. The GitHub commits third — because they were small and fast, the kind of domino that falls in ten minutes and makes you feel human again.

2. The 1-3-5 Rule — The Morning Contract

I began writing a daily contract with myself. One big thing. Three medium things. Five small things. Not a wishlist — a contract. The difference is accountability.

The AI loop actually helps here: I now ask Claude each morning to help me triage the day’s tasks into this structure. It takes four minutes. It saves two hours of drift.

3. The Not-Todo List — The Art of Strategic Abandonment

This one stung.

I identified six recurring tasks that I was doing out of habit, not value. Three I automated. Two I delegated to team members who were frankly better at them than I was. One I simply eliminated — a weekly report nobody was reading.

Freedom, it turns out, is sometimes just a deleted calendar invite.

4. Airplane Mode — The Sacred Window

Between 6:30 AM and 8:00 AM, my phone goes into airplane mode. No Slack. No email. No news. This is when I read, write, and think. The AI loop now lives entirely in this window. Claude gets my full attention. In return, I get my full morning.

5. The 5-Second Rule — Launching Into the Uncomfortable

5-4-3-2-1. Launch.

I use this specifically for the tasks I have been avoiding — the difficult feedback email, the architectural decision document that required me to admit I had been wrong about something for three months. The countdown is ridiculous. It works anyway.

6. S.M.A.R.T Goals — Making the Fuzzy Concrete

My AI reading loop was not SMART. It had no defined endpoint, no measurable output, no time boundary. I added one rule: every reading session must produce one publishable insight within 48 hours. Suddenly, the loop had a shape.

7. The Seesaw System — Balancing the High and the Low

Architecture reviews and PI planning are cognitively heavy. Reviewing pull requests and updating documentation are lighter. I now interleave them deliberately — heavy task, light task, heavy task, light task. My energy curve stopped looking like a cliff and started looking like a wave.

8. The 80/20 Rule — Finding the Vital Few

Twenty percent of my tasks drive eighty percent of my professional impact. For me, that twenty percent is: strategic documents, key stakeholder communications, and the Medium articles that shape my thought leadership positioning.

I put those tasks in the morning. Everything else gets the afternoon.

9. Task Batching — The Context-Switch Tax

Every time you switch contexts, you pay a tax. I was paying it dozens of times a day. Now I batch: all code reviews in one block, all writing in one block, all meetings compressed into Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. The rest of the week breathes.

10. Eat Your Frog — The Hardest Thing First

My frog changes daily. Some days it is a difficult conversation. Some days it is a blank document that needs 800 words I do not yet have. Some days it is simply getting out of bed early enough to have a morning at all.

I eat it first. Always. The rest of the day tastes better for it.

11. The Eisenhower Matrix — Triage as a Discipline

I built a simple habit: every Sunday evening, I run the week’s tasks through the matrix. Urgent + Important gets my mornings. Important + Not Urgent gets scheduled. Urgent + Not Important gets delegated. Not Important + Not Urgent gets deleted without guilt.

The matrix does not give you more time. It gives you better decisions about the time you have.

12. The Unfinished Symphony — The Power of Beginning

I had always been afraid to start things I could not finish in one sitting. The Unfinished Symphony principle inverted this. Now I deliberately start things — a paragraph, a diagram, a code stub — knowing I will not finish them today. The brain, it turns out, does not like loose ends. It works on them in the background, whether you ask it to or not.

Several of my best Medium paragraphs were written in the shower, solving a problem I started the night before.

13. The Pomodoro Technique — Time as Ritual

25 minutes. 5-minute break. Repeat. I pair this with the Airplane Mode window for deep work. What I discovered: the technique is not really about time. It is about permission — permission to stop, permission to rest, permission to begin again.

14. Time Blocking — Designing the Day

My calendar now has three types of blocks: Deep Work (marked in blue, non-negotiable), Collaborative Work (meetings, reviews, team calls), and Recovery (lunch, walk, nothing-in-particular). The third category was the hardest to add. It was the most important.

15. Power Hour + Closing the Day — The Bookends

I begin with a Power Hour: one uninterrupted hour on the week’s most important project. I end with a Closing ritual: wrap up open loops, review what I completed, write three priorities for tomorrow.

The closing ritual, specifically, changed how I sleep. The open loops were not keeping me awake — I had just never given myself a formal place to put them down.

Act IV — What the AI Loop Looks Like Now

The loop did not disappear. It matured.

I still use Claude every morning. I still read, synthesise, and write. But now the loop has a container: it lives in the Airplane Mode window, structured by the 1-3-5 rule, launched by the 5-Second Rule, and bounded by a Power Hour timer. The Eisenhower Matrix decides whether a new reading topic earns a slot in my week. The Domino Effect decides the sequence.

The result: I publish more, drift less, and finish what I start.

The frameworks in Dr. Bada’s cheatsheet are not new ideas. Most of them are decades old. What is new — what I believe is the essential skill for anyone building in the age of AI — is the discipline to apply them when the tools around you are actively rewarding distraction with the illusion of productivity.

Reading faster is not the same as thinking better.

Writing more is not the same as writing well.

A loop that generates output is not the same as a mind that has direction.

Coda — Bringing the House in Order

The Bhagavad Gita speaks of chitta-shuddhi — the purification of the mind, the clearing of the inner house before any great work can be done. I am not a philosopher. I am an engineering manager with a backlog and a calendar and a persistent sense that there is more I could be doing with the hours I have.

But I have come to believe that the frameworks above are a modern chitta-shuddhi. They are not productivity tricks. They are acts of respect — for your own attention, for your team’s time, for the work that deserves to be done well.

The AI will keep reading. The AI will keep writing. The AI will keep suggesting what comes next.

But the architect of that loop — the one who decides what gets built, and when, and why — that has to be you.

Bring your house in order. Then build.
